Field surveys conducted in South African estuaries have provided detailed life-history data for the Southern meagre Argyrosomus hololepidotus. During the 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C] summer spawning season, gravid females exhibit a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%]. The pelagic eggs are released during coastal spawning events, and the embryos develop rapidly within the warm water column. Following a brief incubation period, the yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after just 4 days [ab = 4 days], a developmental speed that is typical for sciaenids spawning in subtropical conditions at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. The hatchlings are initially lecithotrophic, relying entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves. The wet weight at birth is a remarkably small 0.00037 grams [Wwb = 0.00037 grams], reflecting the species' strategy of producing numerous small offspring. This early life stage is characterized by rapid yolk absorption and the swift onset of exogenous feeding in the planktonic environment.

As the yolk-sac larvae exhaust their endogenous reserves, they undergo the trophic switch to first exogenous feeding, marking a critical bottleneck in early survival. The growing pelagic teleost larvae remain in the ichthyoplankton for several weeks, feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton. During this period, the young fish experience substantial allometric growth prior to the metamorphic climax. The maximum recorded longevity for the Southern meagre under natural conditions is estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years], though this figure is based on otolith readings from stable populations at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. This relatively long lifespan is consistent with the species' status as a large-bodied, iteroparous predator within the Sciaenidae family. Research indicates that individuals can ultimately attain a remarkable total length of 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters], making it one of the largest members of its genus. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from the length-weight relationship, reaches approximately 61,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 61,800 grams], highlighting the substantial size variation across the species' life history.

The onset of sexual maturation in Argyrosomus hololepidotus occurs at a clearly defined size threshold rather than a strict chronological age. Analyses of gonadal development in specimens collected from KwaZulu-Natal waters indicate that puberty is attained when individuals reach a total length of 75.4 centimeters [Lp = 75.4 centimeters]. At this length, the calculated wet weight at puberty is approximately 3,100 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,100 grams], signifying a considerable somatic investment before reproductive activity begins. The age at which this size is achieved varies with environmental conditions, but tag-recapture studies suggest it typically requires several years of growth. Once this developmental milestone is reached, the HPG axis activates and gametogenesis commences. This life-history pattern is characteristic of species that maximize lifetime fecundity through repeated, moderate spawning events rather than a single massive reproductive bout.

Investigations of the reproductive biology have confirmed that the Southern meagre follows an iteroparous strategy with multiple spawning events per year. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals asynchronous oocyte development, allowing for the continuous production of egg batches throughout the protracted spawning season. All life-history measurements reported here were collected under estuarine conditions where the ambient water temperature averaged 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], a thermal regime that is optimal for this subtropical sciaenid. The gonadosomatic index of 6% [GSI = 6%] was recorded in spawning females at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. The incubation period for the developing embryos, recorded as 4 days [ab = 4 days] at this temperature, reflects the rapid metabolic rates associated with warm-water development at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. Interestingly, the documented lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] places this species among the longer-lived sciaenids, with the extended reproductive window potentially compensating for the high larval mortality associated with pelagic spawning at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C].

Comparative analyses with congeners reveal that Argyrosomus hololepidotus exhibits one of the largest asymptotic sizes within the genus, with the ultimate total length of 200 cm [Li = 200 cm] being exceeded only by a few Indo-Pacific species. The enormous size range spanned during ontogeny means that an individual's mass increases by over five orders of magnitude from the initial birth weight of only 0.00037 grams [Wwb = 0.00037 grams] to the asymptotic adult mass of 61,800 grams [Wwi = 61,800 grams], a trajectory sustained only in productive estuarine and nearshore environments. The size at puberty, fixed at a total length of 75.4 cm [Lp = 75.4 cm], represents a compromise between the benefits of early reproduction and the advantages of continued somatic growth that enhances future fecundity. At this pubertal size, the wet weight of roughly 3,100 grams [Wwp = roughly 3,100 grams] marks the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult phase. These life-history traits collectively characterize a species well-adapted to the productive, warm-temperate and subtropical waters of the southwestern Indian Ocean.
